items.title: Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age from 536 to around 660 AD
items.note: Tree-ring reconstructions identify a sustained cooling after the 536 and 540 eruptions, framing the plague within a wider climatic crisis.

items.title: People, Plagues, and Prices in the Roman World: The Evidence from Egypt
items.note: Reads Egyptian papyrological prices and wages as showing post-pandemic shifts comparable to those after the Black Death.

items.title: A High-Coverage Yersinia pestis Genome from a Sixth-Century Justinianic Plague Victim
items.note: High-coverage genome from Altenerding, Bavaria, refines the First Pandemic lineage and its relation to modern strains.

items.title: The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire
items.note: Synthesis treating the Justinianic plague and Late Antique cooling as decisive forces in Roman decline.

items.title: Dangers of Noncritical Use of Historical Plague Data
items.who: J. Roosen and D. R. Curtis
items.note: Warns that compiled historical plague datasets carry biases that distort mortality and spread estimates.

items.title: Plagues, climate change, and the end of an empire: A response to Kyle Harper's The Fate of Rome (1–3)
items.note: Three-part critique contesting Harper's use of climate and plague evidence and his causal model of collapse.

items.title: Ancient trash mounds unravel urban collapse a century before the end of Byzantine hegemony in the southern Levant
items.note: Dated refuse mounds at Elusa indicate a mid-sixth-century breakdown of urban waste collection, read as consistent with plague and climate stress.

items.title: Rejecting Catastrophe: The Case of the Justinianic Plague
items.note: Argues the textual evidence for catastrophic mortality is thin and that maximalist narratives rest on circular reasoning.

items.title: Ancient Yersinia pestis genomes from across Western Europe reveal early diversification during the First Pandemic (541–750)
items.note: Eight new genomes from sites including Edix Hill, Britain, show wide geographic reach and lineage diversification during the pandemic.

items.title: The Justinianic Plague: an interdisciplinary review
items.note: Surveys textual, archaeological, genetic and environmental evidence and the gaps between them.

items.title: The Justinianic Plague: An inconsequential pandemic?
items.note: Finds no clear signal of the plague in papyri, legislation, coinage, inscriptions or pollen, challenging the maximalist consensus.

items.title: The 'Justinianic Plague': An "Inconsequential Pandemic"? A Reply
items.note: Rebuts the minimalist PNAS argument, defending a large demographic and cultural impact.

items.title: Modeling the Justinianic Plague: Comparing hypothesized transmission routes
items.who: L. A. White and L. Mordechai
items.note: Compartmental models of Constantinople test bubonic, pneumonic and ectoparasite routes against Procopius's reported mortality.

items.title: The Justinianic Plague and Global Pandemics: The Making of the Plague Concept
items.note: Traces how the Black Death template shaped modern assumptions about the first pandemic's scale.

items.title: New Approaches to the 'Plague of Justinian'
items.note: Defends a significant impact, answering the minimalist critique with legal, papyrological and comparative evidence.

items.title: One Plague for Another? Interdisciplinary Shortcomings in Plague Studies and the Place of the Black Death in Histories of the Justinianic Plague
items.note: Reviews how Black Death analogies have been used in the debate and argues for a shift away from them.

items.title: The First Plague Pandemic in Italy: The Written Evidence
items.note: Catalogues nine to fourteen attested Italian outbreaks across the pandemic and redates Paul the Deacon's 560s plague.

items.title: Dating the Justinianic Plague in England: integrating historical and archaeological data on the early Cambridgeshire region
items.note: Targeted high-precision radiocarbon dates from Edix Hill largely confirm a 540s arrival rather than an earlier presence.

items.title: Contextualising Edix Hill: First-Pandemic Plague and Britain
items.note: Places the Edix Hill aDNA within British textual and archaeological records of early medieval epidemics.

items.title: Challenging the Significance of the LALIA and the Justinianic Plague: A Reanalysis of the Archaeological Record
items.note: Reanalyses Levantine settlement data and finds little archaeological support for sixth-century plague- or climate-driven decline.

items.title: Was the Hephthalite Empire in Central Asia the Cradle of the Justinianic Plague?
items.note: Proposes Hephthalite and Alkhan Huns as conduits carrying plague from Tianshan reservoirs toward the Indian Ocean and Red Sea.

items.title: Genetic Evidence of Yersinia pestis from the First Pandemic
items.note: Reports Y. pestis from a sixth- to seventh-century mass grave at Jerash, the first genomic evidence from the Eastern Mediterranean.

items.title: The First Plague Pandemic in the Byzantine Empire: Toward a New Dynamic Consensus
items.note: Jointly authored by scholars from both sides of the debate, in a themed issue, seeking a regionally variable middle position.

items.title: Bioarchaeological signatures during the Plague of Justinian (541–750 CE) in Jerash (ancient Gerasa), Jordan
items.note: Bioarchaeological analysis of the Jerash mass burial, describing the individuals interred and the context of the grave.

items.title: Evidence for catastrophe at the time of the Plague of Justinian on Bahrain: right time, different disaster
items.note: Bayesian-dated anomalous tombs on Bahrain fall in the early plague years but the authors argue a different catastrophe is likelier.
